Facebook Dating Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Profiles and Protect Yourself

Scammers on Facebook dating profiles are skilled at building trust quickly — but there are clear warning signs that separate genuine users from criminals.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-20 · 9 min read

Facebook dating scam UKfake Facebook dating profileromance scam Facebook
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What is a Facebook dating scam?

A Facebook dating scam happens when a criminal creates a fake profile — often using stolen photos of an attractive person — and targets you through Facebook's dating features or direct messages. The scammer's goal is to build an emotional connection with you over weeks or months, then ask for money. The requests usually start small (a few pounds for a meal or transport) and escalate to larger sums for supposed emergencies, medical bills, business investments, or travel costs to meet you in person.

Some scammers also use the relationship to trick you into sharing personal information, which they then use for identity theft or to blackmail you. The scam is particularly effective because it exploits loneliness and the natural human desire for connection. Victims often feel embarrassed to report it because they have developed genuine feelings for the fake person, even though they have never met in real life.

Warning signs of a fake Facebook dating profile

  • **Stolen or generic photos**: The profile picture looks professionally taken or is a stock image; reverse image search (Google Images) shows the same photo used elsewhere online or on modelling websites.
  • **Vague or inconsistent personal details**: They claim to be a doctor, engineer, or businessman but give evasive answers about their work, location, or family; their story changes slightly each time they tell it.
  • **Reluctance to video call**: They make excuses (broken camera, poor internet, work restrictions) whenever you suggest a video call, voice call, or meeting in person.
  • **Fast emotional escalation**: Within days or weeks they say they love you, want to marry you, or talk about a future together — far faster than a genuine relationship would develop.
  • **Requests for money or financial information**: They ask for cash for emergencies, travel, medical treatment, business opportunities, or to pay off debts; they may also ask for your bank details, card numbers, or passwords.
  • **Isolation tactics**: They discourage you from telling friends or family about the relationship, or they claim your friends are jealous and trying to break you up.
  • **Requests to move off Facebook**: They quickly suggest moving conversations to WhatsApp, Telegram, or email to avoid Facebook's monitoring and reporting systems.
  • **Inconsistent or poor English**: Messages contain spelling errors, awkward phrasing, or copy-paste responses that don't quite fit your question — signs the profile is run by someone for whom English is not a first language or is managed by a team.

How the scam unfolds from first contact to money loss

The scam typically begins when the fake profile sends you a message or likes your photo. They will compliment you, ask personal questions, and seem genuinely interested in getting to know you. Over the following weeks, they build rapport by messaging regularly, sharing (false) details about their life, and expressing affection. They may send you small gifts via Amazon or a delivery service to make the relationship feel real. Once they believe you are emotionally invested, they introduce a problem: a family emergency, a business deal that needs funding, medical bills, or travel costs to visit you.

They ask if you can help with money — often starting with a small amount (£50–£200) to test whether you will comply. If you send money, they thank you profusely and promise to repay you, then create another emergency and ask for more. Some victims have sent thousands of pounds over months. Alternatively, the scammer may ask you to receive money into your bank account on their behalf (claiming they cannot access UK banking), which is a money laundering scheme that can make you liable to the police.

Others use the relationship to extract personal information — your full name, address, date of birth, passport details — which they sell or use for identity theft.

How to verify if a Facebook dating profile is genuine

If you are unsure whether someone is real, take these steps before sharing money or personal information. First, ask them to video call you — use Facebook Messenger's video call feature or suggest WhatsApp video. Genuine people will usually agree; scammers will make excuses. Second, reverse-image search their profile photo: go to Google Images, click the camera icon, and upload or paste their photo URL. If the same image appears on modelling sites, stock photo websites, or other dating profiles, it is stolen.

Third, search their name and any details they have given you (workplace, hometown, university) on Google and social media to see if a real person matches. Fourth, ask specific questions about their life and check if their answers are consistent over time — scammers often slip up or repeat scripted responses. Fifth, be wary if they claim to be a military officer, oil rig worker, or someone in a job that keeps them isolated; these are common cover stories because they explain why they cannot meet or video call easily.

Finally, if they ask for money, that is a definitive red flag — genuine people do not ask strangers for cash, no matter how close you feel.

What to do immediately if you have already sent money or shared details

If you have sent money, contact your bank or payment service right away — the sooner you report it, the better the chance of recovering the funds. Call the number on the back of your card or use your banking app to report the transaction as fraudulent. If you used a money transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram, contact them immediately to try to stop the payment. If you paid via PayPal, report it as an unauthorised transaction.

Report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.org.uk — this creates an official record and helps the police identify patterns. If you have shared personal information (name, address, date of birth, passport details, bank account number), contact Cifas, the UK's fraud prevention service, to register for identity theft protection. Monitor your credit file using a free service like Clearscore or Experian to spot any fraudulent accounts opened in your name.

If the scammer has explicit photos or videos of you, report them to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk and to Facebook directly using the report button on their profile. Do not send any more money, even if they claim they will repay you or that you owe them — this is a common manipulation tactic.

Reporting the scam in the UK

Report the fake profile to Facebook immediately by clicking the three dots on their profile, selecting 'Report', and choosing 'It's a fake account' or 'It's a scam'. Facebook will investigate and may remove the profile, though this can take time. Report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or at reportfraud.org.uk — they handle fraud reports for the UK and share information with law enforcement. If you received suspicious messages or links, forward them to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If the scammer sent you spam text messages, forward them to 7726 (spamming).

Contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 if you need support understanding your rights or next steps. If you believe your identity has been stolen, report it to Action Fraud (part of Report Fraud) and ask for a crime reference number — you will need this if you want to dispute fraudulent accounts or claims. Keep all messages, screenshots, and transaction records as evidence for the police and your bank. The more people who report the same profile, the faster Facebook and law enforcement can act.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get my money back if I sent it to a Facebook dating scammer?

It depends on how you paid. If you used a bank transfer or debit card, contact your bank immediately — they may be able to reverse the transaction if you report it quickly, especially if the money has not yet been withdrawn. If you used a money transfer service like Western Union, contact them urgently to try to stop the payment. PayPal disputes can sometimes be won if you report it as an unauthorised transaction. However, if the money has already been collected and the scammer is abroad, recovery is unlikely. Report it to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) and your bank regardless — they will investigate and may recover funds in some cases.

What should I do if the scammer is threatening me or asking me to send explicit photos?

Do not send any photos or videos, and do not respond to threats. Block the profile immediately on Facebook and any other platform they are using. If they are threatening to harm you or blackmail you with intimate images, report it to the police by calling 101 (non-emergency) or 999 if you are in immediate danger. Report the profile to Facebook and to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk if they have shared explicit content of you. If the threats are serious or ongoing, contact your local police station or Victim Support (0808 168 9111) for help.

Is it safe to meet someone from a Facebook dating profile in person?

Meeting someone you have only known online carries risks, especially if you have not video called them first. Before meeting anyone, verify their identity by video call and reverse-image search their photos. If you do decide to meet, tell a trusted friend or family member where you are going, who you are meeting, and when you expect to be back. Meet in a public place during daylight hours, not at their home or a private location. If anything feels wrong or they do not match their photos, leave immediately. If they ask for money before or during the meeting, that is a scam — genuine people do not do this.

How can I tell if someone's Facebook profile is real before I start chatting?

Check their profile for these signs of authenticity: a long history of posts and photos (scammers often have very few), tagged photos from friends (showing they have a real social circle), consistent details across their profile, and a profile picture that matches their other photos. Reverse-image search their main photo using Google Images — if it appears on modelling sites or other dating profiles, it is fake. Look at their friends list; if they have very few friends or all their friends are also attractive singles with minimal activity, the profile is likely fake. Real people usually have a mix of friends, family, and colleagues. If something feels off, trust your instinct and do not engage.

What if I have already fallen in love with someone and now I am worried they might be a scammer?

It is painful, but ask them to video call you — this is the quickest way to verify they are real. If they refuse or make excuses, that is a strong warning sign. Ask specific questions about their life and check if the answers are consistent. Search their name and details online. If they ask for money at any point, that is a definitive red flag — genuine partners do not ask strangers for cash. Talk to a trusted friend or family member about your concerns; they may spot things you have missed because you are emotionally involved. If you are struggling with the emotional impact, contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) or Victim Support (0808 168 9111) for confidential support.
